source.title: Opening the Black Box: predicting the trainability of deep neural networks with reconstruction entropy
source.authors: Yanick Thurn; R. Jefferson; Johanna Erdmenger

record.tranche_reason: The study compares trained-network accuracy across random weight-variance settings to assess trainability, using reconstruction entropy as a proxy rather than directly measuring training classification error or the initialization methods named in the versions.
record.gate_note: The reported accuracy sweep bears on initialization-dependent trainability. Reconstruction-entropy curves, ResNet/CNN predictions, and timing benchmarks do not independently measure the claim’s training-error outcome. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: Figure 3 reports the study's own trained-network accuracy across Gaussian initialization variances and depths on MNIST. This bears on V4's initialization-dependent trainable depth, alongside the study's new reconstruction-entropy predictor. The entropy predictions alone would not test V4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that reconstruction entropy predicts trainable initialization regions before training the target network, and report qualitative agreement with their MNIST accuracy sweep. They also claim computational savings and interpretable reconstructions. Prediction does not guarantee successful training under arbitrary hyperparameters.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses random tanh feedforward networks and sweeps weight and bias variances, then compares final accuracy with an entropy-based trainability proxy. It does not reproduce the specific initialization comparisons in V4.
record.method_sensitivity: The cutoff depends on the numerical threshold η; the authors report the ordered phase is less sensitive to this choice than the chaotic phase. The chaotic-phase differential-entropy result is sensitive to residual information and training duration.

fits_no_version.finding: Reconstruction-entropy profiles predict information-preserving regions for untrained MLPs, ResNets, CNNs, and white-noise inputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reconstruction entropy can predict initialization-dependent trainability before training the target network.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 1 benchmarks reconstruction-based prediction time against target-network epoch time.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Auxiliary reconstruction networks can reduce the computational cost of selecting initializations.

record.problems: The accuracy results bearing on initialization-dependent trainability appear in a figure without extractable values in the supplied text. The authors state that trainability assessment depends on the maximum training epochs and that hyperparameters such as learning rate and batch size matter. The entropy proxy is described as necessary but not sufficient for trainability.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted; the relevant accuracy sweep is figure-only and its values cannot be extracted from the supplied text.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error in large convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, random labels, and the specified capacity and training-recipe comparisons.
Teacher-student ReLU optimization, spurious local minima, and the effect of extra student neurons.
Training-error degradation with depth in plain convolutional networks, its prevention by identity shortcuts, and the special initialization and Fixup cases.

Direct training-speed comparisons; activation-matched versus mismatched initializations; direct measurements of vanishing or exploding gradients; orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization; and training 10,000-layer convolutional networks.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, catapult recovery, sharpness trajectories, and divergence.
Accuracy gain and learning-rate tolerance with versus without batch normalization, including Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The declared figure-only accuracy sweep is not an additional missing result. Entropy-threshold sensitivity concerns the predictor and does not independently limit V4. Figure 3 does not specify whether accuracy is measured on training or held-out data, so it cannot establish V1's training-error outcome.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not report training classification error, zero or near-zero training error, corrupted or random labels, CIFAR-100, or comparisons with smaller models, early stopping, or regularized recipes.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student problem, spurious-minimum rate, or student-width comparison.
No comparison of plain and identity-shortcut networks on training error, and no test of the cited special initializations or normalization-free residual recipe.

The MNIST accuracy-versus-weight-variance sweep bears on initialization-dependent trainability, but the paper reports its accuracy values only in a figure. It does not compare activation-matched with mismatched initializations, Gaussian with orthogonal weights, or training speed and trainable depth across those initialization methods.
No learning-rate stability threshold, loss rise and recovery, sharpness tracking, or divergence comparison.
No batch-normalization comparison or test of normalization-free residual training.

relationships.condition: Plain Gaussian-initialized tanh networks on MNIST, varying weight variance and depth at bias variance 0.05, with learning rate 0.001 and a 200-epoch budget.
relationships.reason: Based on Section 2.1 and Figure 3's textual description, final accuracy identifies a trainable critical regime agreeing with preserved signal propagation. No row IDs exist: the record explicitly declares this figure-only accuracy sweep, and numerical accuracies are unavailable.
relationships.display_finding: Final accuracy identified a trainable critical regime consistent with preserved signal propagation.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
